questions.q: What is the article mainly about?
options: Ukraine opening its battlefield data to allies to train A.I. weapons
Russian efforts to build drone factories for autonomous weapons
How ChatGPT and other chatbots are trained on human writing
A new treaty banning fully autonomous weapons worldwide
questions.explain: Ukraine's Avenger Labs shares war data with allied firms to develop A.I. weapons.

questions.q: What must companies give Ukraine in return for the free data?
options: Licenses to any software they develop
Cash royalties on each drone they sell
Shared access to their own battlefield data
Equity stakes in their companies
questions.explain: Data is free but companies must give the Ukrainian military licenses to the software.

questions.q: What problem did Anna Bacciarelli highlight about A.I. models used in weapons?
options: They often require human pilots to confirm targets
Their internal reasoning is opaque, obscuring accountability
They are too slow to process real-time battlefield footage
They depend on expensive cloud infrastructure outside Ukraine
questions.explain: She said the 'black box obscures accountability' because internal reasoning is opaque.

questions.q: How many drone surveillance and strike videos does Avenger Labs hold?
options: Over five million
About 500,000
Over fifty million
Around 50,000
questions.explain: It holds more than five million drone surveillance and strike videos.

questions.q: What limitation does Kateryna Bondar raise?
options: Licensing fees make the data too expensive for smaller allies
Many of the videos are staged simulations, not real combat
The cloud platform is not encrypted and could be hacked
Data on Russian assets may not transfer to other conflicts
questions.explain: She asks what use training on Russian assets is away from Ukraine, e.g. in a Middle East war.
